utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, registrar. I would like to greet on Wednesday, the 13th of February, 2008, the witness representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation, Mr. President. Since you started speaking I've heard nothing. Nothing has been interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation. [B/C/S on English channel] So it's working now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that after having greeted all and everyone, we shall resume with the cross-examination, and I indicated yesterday that Mr. Seselj had three hours and eight minutes left if I'm not mistaken. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I have to provide you with a short piece of information. Yesterday I talked to Boris Petrov from the secretary, from the registry about financing my defence and he briefly told me that the registry has no intention of financing the Defence comprehensively, but from now on and he said that -- expressly that they did not intend to finance the pre-trial stage. And he also said that, in that way, that is how they in fact interpret your ruling and decision. Thank you. That was my duty to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this matter I would like to remind my colleagues or those people that know about it and those that don't, a long time ago when this case was in the hands of Trial Chamber II, I was a member of this Trial Chamber, you had filed a motion seeking leave for reimbursement of all your expenses involved in the preparation of your defence. If I remember correctly this amounted to several million euros, but I don't have the exact figure at hand. At the time, Trial Chamber II was supposed to hand down a decision on this matter. Personally, this is something I told you at a Pre-Trial Conference, a Status Conference. I had my own personal view on the matter, but I was unable to have my personal view recorded, because in the meantime this case had been referred to Trial Chamber III or I. I don't remember which. Therefore, Trial Chamber II had not responded to your application. In the decision handed down by this Chamber on the preparation of your defence, we did not address this issue. If you now wish this to be applied retroactively, you should then file a motion and ask the registrar to reimburse you all those expenses involved before the decision was taken and the Trial Chamber will then rule on the matter. That is all I can say about this which relates to the retroactive application of our decision. We shall now move on to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-004, you gave two statements to The Hague Tribunal, is that right, or have you given more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One of them was on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of May, 2002, and the second one was on the 1st and 2nd and 14th of August, 2006; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 2006 they in fact informed you that your first statement could be used in the trial against me; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At the time, you said that you weren't ready to testify in the criminal proceedings against me; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say that because you considered that there was any -- that I posed any danger to you, that there was a threat from me to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from you personally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or perhaps from people from the Serbian Radical Party whose president I am or somebody close to me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say specifically who I expected unpleasantness from, but since I did experience unpleasantness on the streets of Belgrade previously, I wanted to protect my family from any incidents or any attacks whether through the sympathisers of your -- your party, but as far as you're personally concerned, I didn't say that I would have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that new statement, you once again spoke about my arrival in Western Slavonia, and you have come to Hague on two occasions since the new year to testify; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first time you did not arrive because some other witnesses took longer with their testimony and now it's your turn finally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At the time did the Prosecution hold proofing sessions with you to prepare you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did those proofing sessions last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they lasted one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One day upon your first arrival and one day when you arrived the second time or a total of one day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A total of one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you calculate this in terms of hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps five or six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that five- or six-hour interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for me to remember and remind myself of what I said in my statement, to take a look at some documents again, to refresh my memory with respect to the proceedings going on here today, and we went through some of the events that took place on the basis of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the representative of the OTP tell you what questions you might expect from me during the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said here that I came to Western Slavonia at the end of October or the beginning of November 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can I remind you and tell you that it was on the 18th of November that I in fact arrived in Banja Luka by a -- and I was flown in there in a JNA helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that with me from Belgrade Ilija Sasic came, your Foreign Minister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Sasic did come together with you but he wasn't Foreign Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a member of the government. I thought he was the Foreign Minister.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that government did not function like a proper government, and Mr. Ilija Sasic was an independent man or somebody whom Veljko Vukelic placed his trust in. He was a lone rider, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the very fact that I came in a JNA helicopter testifies to the fact that I didn't come on a private visit; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it would appear, although I don't know what kind of organisation it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Two officers, two JNA officers, came with me and the helicopter pilots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's how it was, then that's probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The day I arrived, I held a rally in the large hall of Borik, called Borik, in Banja Luka. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you attended the meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were interested in hearing what I had to say. It had importance to you since you came to the rally from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I happened to be in Banja Luka at the time, and I heard about the rally, so I decided to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you remember some of the positions I put forward at the rally if I remind you of certain fragments of what I said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say that I don't remember what you actually said, but you can of course remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for you to remember after all those years without me reminding you or without the Prosecution reminding you. It's difficult to remember all the details, I'm fully conscious of that, but do you remember that a great part of my speech was focused on saying that a civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be avoided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you also remember that I said that the only chance to preserve peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina was for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within the composition of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember my saying that that was the only chance for both the Serbs and the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina to avoid what was happening in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you said something along those lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So although I was belligerent in the areas that there was a war going on, that is to say I wanted victory, but where there wasn't a war going on I wished for peace? Is that the conclusion that you could draw from my speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since I came in a JNA helicopter with Ilija Sasic, I came alone; I had no escort, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Therefore, I could not have had any export -- escort when I reached Western Slavonia, and in your statement it says that seven or eight persons escorted me. It was only the locals from Western Slavonia that could have escorted me who had greeted me there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you weren't alone. I didn't say that you had escorts in the sense of any officers acting as your escorts. There was other people with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if I were going there myself and I've never been to Western Slavonia before I would have lost my way, so somebody had to go with me to show me where to go; am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Somebody had to drive me, too, I couldn't go on foot could I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. You couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And from Banja Luka on the first day Nikodin Cavic came with me. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by name. I can't remember who the man was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me remind you. He was the founder of the Serbian Radical Party in Banja Luka at the time and he organised this particular rally in the Borik hall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now. Nikodin, yes, I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He brought me to Western Slavonia and went back the same day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here in your statement in several -- in several places that Veljko Vukelic was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But then the Prosecution itself cautions you and says that the commander of the Territorial Defence was in fact Colonel Trbojevic and not Veljko Vukelic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at the beginning from August and maybe even before August I'm not quite sure when right up until the end of October and the beginning of November, Mr. Vukelic was the commander of Western Slavonia, and then he withdrew. He knows the reasons for that himself, and that post was taken over by Mr. Jovan Trbojevic when he came from Belgrade and said that he had been sent by the leaders of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you that Jovan Trbojevic arrived in Western Slavonia somewhat earlier not as you said at the end of October; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact date when Mr. Trbojevic arrived, but I do know that on the 15th of October when the first exodus took place from Grubisno Polje that he was still the commander -- or, rather, Veljko Vukelic was still the commander and that went on for several more weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say the 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see, the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of October was when the first exodus from Grubisno Polje took place and at that time the commander was still Veljko Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that by law the armed forces of the SFRY were united?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that the JNA and the Territorial Defence had one General Staff of the armed forces in Belgrade, one body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Therefore, the fact that you -- the JNA had sent Colonel Trbojevic to be commander of the Territorial Defence is the best proof that the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia was within the composition of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was able to see that later on when the JNA came to the Okucani area. What their communication was before that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Until the JNA took over the Territorial Defence there were spontaneous forms of organisation on the part of the Serbian population in Western Slavonia; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were organised by the Territorial Defence and I've already mentioned that with the Secretariat of Defence. I don't know how they were organised or who organised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party exclusively arrived in -- arrived in Western Slavonia exclusively through the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that from the media. I heard you giving statements that this was a joint action with the JNA, but I don't know how it was specifically organised and who arranged this and in what way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You will remember that at the time Bosnia-Herzegovina was still not at war, but the police forces have already been strengthened and the Territorial Defence and certain paramilitary formations began to appear in different parts; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, how could the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party be able to pass through Posavina had they not moved in a JNA column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they needed some sort of escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Posavina there were a lot of Muslims and Croats living there. There were municipalities where the Croats were in the majority and other municipalities where the Muslim population was in the majority; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And if it had not been organised by the JNA, our volunteers had to fight to make their advancement. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the circumstances would be. All I can say is that in the JNA of the day which was there and the Banja Luka Corps was there, there were both Muslims and Croats, Croat soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that among the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there were also Muslims and Catholics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Radovan Novacic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the commander of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in Western Slavonia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard something like that, referring to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that his father is a Croat and his mother a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And if that is true, what I'm saying is correct, does that then mean that we sent a man like that over there not in the desire perpetrating crimes against the Croatian population but quite the opposite, that fighting should be against the enemy and protect the entire civilian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it should have been because the man was from a mixed marriage so one had to take into -- or rather one had to take care of all people of different faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he had no reason to hate the Croats and Catholics but he was against those who wished to break up Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So while I can't say what he advocated specifically or what he thought, but one might conclude it was as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were regularly paid by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but that's what people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the members of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia were paid by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The salaries were small, but they still meant something; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It meant something to people at the time as they had no other source of income.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the territory of Western Slavonia territorially within the remit of the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what transpired. Some 30 days after the beginning of the war, the Banja Luka Corps moved to Western Slavonia and took the Territorial Defence under its wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know anything the organisation of the Territorial Defence of the JNA before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't familiar with that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you serve in the army? Did you do a military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that there used to be military districts of the JNA, the Zagreb, Sarajevo, Belgrade district and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in the late '80s this was reorganised so there were three strategic groups.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember while the Sarajevo army district was still in existence with its headquarters in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it also encompassed almost all of Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware that every volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party has had his war service recognised based on his participation in the events in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can conclude that because the territorials did the same. They also asked to have their service in the war recognised as a length of service for pension purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there's a length of service in wartime and length of service in employment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The former is inscribed in the work booklet and the latter in the military booklet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who were wounded in the fighting immediately regulated all their benefits as war invalids, all their entitlements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that specifically but I do know that some who were wounded or became invalids from the Territorial Defence managed to secure their rights, so if the -- if the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were under JNA command, they would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that they were put on an equal footing with JNA soldiers as regards their entitlements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that when a volunteer of the SRS was killed in Western Slavonia the JNA organised the transport of the body to Serbia to his place of birth and that a military band, the military band of the local garrison would play at the funeral and that salvo would be fired in his honour by the members of the garrison as if an active duty soldier had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that myself, however, one might conclude that because that's how it happened in the case of the territorials. I attended a few funerals of young men killed around Okucani and they were buried with military honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that some Serbs, along with some Croats, when they heard that Seselj's men had arrived began leaving the area because they were afraid of my men. Can you give me the name of a Serb who was frightened by volunteers of the SRS and left Western Slavonia for that reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. As regards a name I was told that personally by a man called Luka Krajinovic. Unfortunately he's deceased now. But in answer to your question I can give you a specific name. He told me he was afraid, that he had had an encounter. I don't know what sort of encounter, but that's what I heard from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a high-ranking official of the civilian authorities in Western Slavonia, you did not draw distinctions on the ground between volunteers of the SRS and other volunteers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not really an official at the time because it all functioned through Territorial Defence Staffs, but I did have the respect of the local people and some authority among them. However, I didn't have contact with the volunteers. I didn't know who came from where. They didn't confide in me and I didn't ask them any questions. So I thought they were all one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if you did not draw distinctions, how much more difficult was it for ordinary citizens to draw that distinction? Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that ordinary people couldn't really draw these distinctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Hague investigators asked you about General Dusan Pekic. You know who Dusan Pekic is; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he comes from the Banija area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's a national hero from World War II, a general of the JNA and he was the president of the veterans association after the war of liberation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that he was one of the officials of the Association of Serbs from Croatia with its headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the SRS from the very beginning cooperated with that association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you were living in Western Slavonia, are you able to draw a distinction between the activities of volunteers of the SRS in the spring of -- from the spring of 1991 to September 1991 and from September 1991, when the JNA joined in the fighting or not? Can you draw this distinction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have now given me specific time periods, but this was all a very short period of time, and right now I wouldn't dare try to draw that kind of distinction. Everything was very chaotic down there. A lot of things happened in a short space of time. So these nuances you are referring to are something that I really cannot talk about right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In -- do you know that in early February -- in February and March 1991, a delegation of prominent Serbs from Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem arrived to see me in Belgrade asking that the Serb Radical Party send volunteers to participate in the defence imperiled Serbian villages in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something about this from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 9th of March I visited several Serb villages in Eastern Slavonia which were thought to be the most under threat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that because on the 9th of March I was in Pakrac engaged in difficult negotiations with representatives of the Croatian authorities so I was unable to follow up other events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that right after that we started sending volunteers to Eastern Slavonia, to the villages there and to villages in Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that volunteers had arrived there but I can't tell you in what time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And could you link my statements that I was in command in -- of those volunteers to the period when the JNA was not yet participating in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you did make such statements at that time, and the JNA wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear me saying that I was the commander after the JNA became involved in the fighting and the volunteers acted exclusively within the organisation of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't hear me representing myself as a commander in public then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that some time in early September the General Staff of the armed forces of Yugoslavia issued an edict about the deployment of volunteers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've been asked a series of questions that I find of great importance. Let's try to expand on your answers. Please tell me if you served, if you did your military service in the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long did it last, this military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A year, but I had some leave granted as a reward, so I left a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on this brief experience of one year in the JNA, do you think that it is possible for there to be a double chain of command in the JNA military chain of command on the one hand and political chain of command on the other hand based on a political party, and this political chain of command would be beside the military chain of command? Would that be possible according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was one military command. I didn't really understand your question when you say a political party. There was one party at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be more specific. When you were a soldier of the JNA, were you supposed to obey the orders of the military authority or the orders of a political party that you might be a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, every soldier has to obey the orders issued by his immediate superior. He only listens to the military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you yourself served in the JNA, were you a member of a political party at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I was a member of the League of Communists. There was only one political party then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time you were a member of the League of Communists as part of your military occupation and the military occupation of your fellow soldiers and officers of the JNA, was there a permanent connection with the League of Communists in order to decide what sort of behaviour should be yours, or was the only connection or contact you had with the military chain of command or hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a connection exclusively with the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's precisely why I insist on the distinction between these two periods, the period when the JNA did not participate in the fighting and the period when it did, so that you and your colleagues can understand what this is all about. That's why I'm insisting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Arming was mentioned here, arming of Serb units of the Territorial Defence in Serb area, and you were asked whether General Dusan Pekic participated in the arming of people from Western Slavonia and your response was that you didn't have any information about that, but you did learn from the media that he was involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible that because you didn't understand the question you gave an erroneous answer or because you were under the influence of the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered the question by saying that at the beginning when the arming started I don't know who organised it or how it proceeded. Later on I heard that Mr. Pekic had participated in it. I never attended a meeting where he agreed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The OTP showed you here and probably earlier as well a clip from the BBC broadcast on "The Death of Yugoslavia" where I am attacking Radmilo Bogdanovic, the former minister of police of Serbia, saying that he had given weapons to armed volunteers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that that conversation was conducted in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe me, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But if I tell you that and the OTP does have the information when the conversation was conducted, you have no reason to disbelieve me. Do you remember that in 1995 I personally and the entire SRS were involved in a fierce political showdown with Milosevic, Slobodan Milosevic, and his regime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Serbian political life, was it common when there is such a showdown for both sides to launch smokescreens, to introduce confusion into the public mind and say something detrimental to their opponents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You remember that Milosevic's regime also said about me that I was a criminal or an alcoholic. I almost never drink alcohol, but I was publicly accused of being an alcoholic. I couldn't go from one newspaper reader to another explaining I wasn't; is that right? Do you remember those attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'm just waiting for the interpretation to finish before I start replying. Yes, I remember. They were very aggressive attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At dinner in Zvecevo which you also attended, did I drink any alcohol at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me I don't remember. If you say so, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, some people drank and did they joke about me because I wasn't drinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't matter. You're aware that in those political showdowns on both sides things were launched -- statements were launched which did not fully correspond to the facts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I would be falsely accused of something and I would respond imaginatively, launching a series of accusations against the leader of the regime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you were very imaginative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had some experience with my imagination, didn't you, my imaginativeness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I had a special reason to criticise the Milosevic regime at the time, because they were then conducting a so-called peace-making policy, blockading Republika Srpska, and they started accepting all the so-called Western peace initiatives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time Mr. Slobodan Milosevic was making efforts to have adopted certain plans that the West demanded of him and you opposed that policy of his at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that in late 1994, early 1995 for four months I was in Milosevic's prison and then in the summer of 1995, a further two months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember you were imprisoned but I don't know exactly for how long. But I know that you spent some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's up to me to remember how long. At that time did I then have any reason to spare Milosevic and his regime if I had been repeatedly imprisoned illegally, unlawfully?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that you had good reason to be angry and to hit back, to lash out the way you did because he kept you in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I have another reason to put up this smokescreen, that Radmilo Bogdanovic had collected arms for the Territorial Defence and the volunteers in order to cover up who really did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's possible. You know best the reasons and the causes, but the reason for your imprisonment might be what you said about Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the reason was to hide from the public that it was actually Zoran Pekic who organised the arming of the Territorial Defence and volunteers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course I didn't mention General Dusan Pekic, but he died two months ago, so he's quite safe. Now nobody can imprison him any longer or do anything else. Do you know he died two months ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know it was absolutely the oldest weaponry from the depots of the Territorial Defence? It was scraping the barrel. Thompsons from the Second World War, automatic rifles, Spagin of the Soviet army, M-48s, M-56s. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard people complaining they had received old weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's obvious that through General Pekic we were able to get weaponry from the JNA that the JNA had written off a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say now that it was the only way to get the weapons, but if it was that old, it had probably been written off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Territorial Defence and volunteers did get modern weapons, especially the Kalashnikovs and similar, only when the JNA got involved in the armed conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was noticed later that modern weapons appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean after August 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there, too, we see a significant difference between the period of self-organisation of Serbian territorials in Slavonia, the engagement of the Serbian Radical Party in the first period versus the period when the JNA got involved in the combat and when each of my political speeches pointed out that we were all one single army. We were all the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said that it was a single army. It was all the JNA, that your volunteers were under the command of the JNA. You did make statements of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a single case in any theatre of war where volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party showed up outside JNA units after the 1st of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't have insight into the broader region except my part of Western Slavonia, especially during the war. It's difficult even for local people to move around let alone me, an outsider, but I knew about Western Slavonia, and that was true enough there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say to ICTY investigators that I was responsible for the killing of Croat civilians in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said you were responsible. I said I had heard that volunteers were involved in that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then ICTY investigators put it in a statement that you signed that you thought I was responsible for the killings in Vocin. That's page 5, beginning of paragraph 2. And that the reason why you think so is that it was well known I had come to inspect my units in Vocin. Is that something the investigators and the Prosecutors put in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that a lot. I said I had heard volunteers were involved. I said you had come to inspect your volunteers in the area of Vocin. You visited them. But I didn't say that you had ordered that killing or that you were directly responsible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's the Prosecutors of the Tribunal who arbitrarily put this in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way the statement was written. That's what they understood probably from the discussion we had, but I never directly accused you of being responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's because you didn't write the statement. They wrote the statement on the basis of your interview and gave it to you to sign.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked. They drafted a statement and I signed the statement after reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that a unit of volunteers was present somewhere in the area around Vocin; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know it was about ten kilometres away from Vocin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the exact location, so I can't tell you the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But if you had checked where that unit was, if you had gone to that location to see the unit, to see those men, do you think you would have been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would have been killed, although I was not really well-liked among the militaries, but I don't think they would have actually killed me. I can't tell you. I didn't think about that much. They had no reason to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But The Hague Prosecutors put it in your statement that you had been there to check, that in fact that if you had gone there to check that the volunteer unit was there in Vocin or around Vocin, you would probably have been killed. That's in your statement of August.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you why it was written that way, I think. Jovo Vezmar who was in the staff of the Territorial Defence for Western Slavonia warned me that I should have no contact with military units or try to inspect them, because I had had one contact at the very outset. So he invited me to the staff and told me that if I try that again, I would be killed, and that's why I thought that if I had tried to make another contact of that kind, this promise made by one of the commanders would have been made true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he is from Pakrac. He has nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's from Pakrac. He was first commander of the TO staff of Pakrac, and he was later with the staff of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were never in danger at that time to be killed by me or the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Vezmar threatened me directly in a way that you or your volunteers never did. Not in the words that Jovo Vezmar and other people from the TO did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1991 did I ever intervene in your interpersonal conflicts in Western Slavonia? I mean conflicts between Serbian leaders, politicians, whatever you want to call them. Did I get involved in that in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When you were there and just at that time, you did not get involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At that dinner in Zvecevo, did I greet you cordially like everyone else, and was it generally cordial conversation as a whole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was correct. There were no incidents. There were no quarrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you then conclude that I had no prejudice or animosity towards any of you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here in the statement that you gave on the 14th of August, 2006, you said that as far as you knew, in Western Slavonia there were only volunteers linked to the Serbian Radical Party, and there were no volunteers linked to other political parties. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that because nobody else ever appeared or ever made any claims to any volunteers. That's why I concluded that they were all volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, and that was the general opinion in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, a few years earlier, in the statement from year 2002, on page 30 you say: "There existed a unit of White Eagles in Vocin and another one in Kamenska numbering around 30 men. It was said that there was a unit of the Serbian guards of Vuk Draskovic. I had no contact with those people." You stated that in 2002 when your memory was fresher than in 2006; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that statement I gave in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So were there any White Eagles in Western Slavonia or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later gave that statement that I did because it was always said that there were volunteers of only one organisation. White Eagles were mentioned, and I said I didn't see them myself. I just heard about them, and to whom they belonged I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you know that there were in Kamenska around 30 men belonging to White Eagles. That's what you said in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the general talk mentioning that number and those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who brought White Eagles to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many times did you meet General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When in early 1992 you publicly blamed a crime on the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, I attacked you and General Aleksandar Vasiljevic by saying that you had brought White Eagles to Western Slavonia. I'm not asking if this is the truth. I'm asking if I did make that accusation against you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You accused me of being responsible for what happened in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember I also mentioned General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember you mentioned him, but I don't remember you put me and him in the same context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that it hasn't been elucidated to date how exactly the White Eagles came to Western Slavonia? The volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party went to the barracks of the JNA in Bubanj Potok. They got uniforms there. Sometimes they got weapons there too. Sometimes the weapons were given later in Okucani. And all of them went along the same channel. The White Eagles never passed through the Bubanj Potok barracks. To date it's not exactly known how they turned up in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you say, it hasn't been elucidated to date and that might make it easier for you to understand that we, at the time, didn't know how they came, who organised it, and at the time I didn't know who brought them and on whose orders they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But when you blamed that crime in Vocin on the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, you did that randomly, without any verifiable information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no investigation at the time if you mean that I could have used reliable information from an inquiry. I heard from people who had come from that area that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party participated in the liquidation of those people. Now, which exactly volunteers and who specifically was there I don't know. I just said what I had heard. I didn't mention any investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you did mention the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, and that's why I lashed out saying that you were responsible for the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I lashed out at you naming your volunteers, and then you hit back linking me with the White Eagles. You made these statements in the media like I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come that in 2002 you spoke about the existence of White Eagle units, namely two units, you even mentioned the Serbian guards of Vuk Draskovic, and then in the statement of 2006 you denied that there were any other volunteers but those from the Serbian Radical Party? Is that a suggestion The Hague Prosecutors made or did they simply write it on their own in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not suggest it, and they didn't write my statement. I wrote my own statement. Nobody imposed anything on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then how do you explain the significant discrepancy between the two statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before my first statement, I learned from talking to someone that the White Eagles and the guards were mentioned. That's why it stayed in my mind. You said yourself that the situation was very confused. I didn't realise it was very important that I mentioned other volunteers. You say that there is a lot of guessing and speculation to this day. But since there were no other leaders representing the White Eagles or any other organisation, it was thought that all of the volunteers were from one and the same source. Maybe I was also impressed by that movie where you spoke about the White Eagles, and based on that, too, I concluded that all those volunteers were together in the same basket. You saw yourself those White Eagles, those volunteers with the White Eagle on their helmets. That probably led me to conclude what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you make a distinction between the two-headed white eagle as an old ancient Serbian symbol back from the dynasty of the Nemanjics taken over from the Byzantine tradition - it is still the official Serbian symbol on the flag and the coat of arms - and a specific organisation called the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the state official symbols are one thing and White Eagles as volunteers are something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear me denying in public that the crimes against Croat civilians in Western Slavonia happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear you denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear me blaming that crime publicly on the White Eagles directly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You saw yesterday that document shown to you by the Prosecution listing 68 suspects for the crimes in Vocin and other places. Did you see that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you see that there were only names of local residents of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think at the beginning when those Puces [phoen] were being mentioned, they were not residents of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party on that list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who belonged to what organisation there, so I can't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that when I was in Western Slavonia when I publicly spoke that I advocated the expulsion of the Croatian population from Western Slavonia? Did you hear me say that ever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But here they slipped into your statement of 206 on page 6, paragraph 14, that -- that I said that the best thing for the Croats would be for them to go to Croatia, and that means that a Greater Serbia would be a state of Serbs alone. And that is to be found on page 6 of your 206 statement. Did you say that or did they put that in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was on the basis of the footage we saw when there was mention of the Croatian state and that that's where that conclusion came from. On the basis of the video that was shown of your speech, how a Croatian state should be formed and who should live in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you said in examination-in-chief yourself that I considered that the majority of today's alleged Croats were in fact the Serb Catholics and that the Bosnian Muslims were Serbs of the Islamic faith; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in your region in Western Slavonia, for instance, for Slavonian Catholics were they referred to as being Sokci? Was that term used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what does Sokac mean? Can you explain that to us? What does that term mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the Croats over there, they -- it was considered that Empress Marija Terezija had converted them to Catholicism but previously they had been Orthodox and that was in those villages and that some of them had taken over the Catholic faith; some remained Greco-Catholic, some took over the Roman Catholic faith entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they were Orthodox Serbs at one time who converted to Catholicism and the other Serb Orthodox referred to these people as the Sokci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that was the reason for them being Sokci, but as I said some convert from orthodoxy to the Roman Catholic faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you are an educated man, the Orthodox Serbs make the sign of the cross using three fingers; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Whereas the Catholics make the sign of the cross with all five fingers and a straight palm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, through history, was that a slightly derogatory way of making the sign of the cross if you use five fingers and your whole hand, meaning a Saka, hand, and then later on this became Sokci, from Saka, the word Saka. Is that how that name came to be used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one possible interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you come across this explanation in books, in literature. Saka and Sakci becoming Sokci. Is it true that I always said that the Sokci from Slavonia were Serbs of the Catholic faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You also spoke about the Uliac [phoen] and you know about the Zumberacka union; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the environs in Zagreb, do these Greco-Catholics still exist who have Orthodox ceremonies, religious ceremonies but recognise the Pope as the head of the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And today on Croatian television we sometimes see their prayers being said. I watch programmes like that in the detention centre, in prison here. I watch Croatian television broadcasting that kind of programme; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the religious ceremony is completely Orthodox but they mention the Pope in their prayers and they mostly consider themselves to be Croats; rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in Croatia today, is the process being continued of converting Serbs to the Roman Catholic faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that does occur, it is on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course it's on an individual basis. Each man has to decide for himself. But do you know the official date of the Serbian Catholic church whereby over 30.000 Orthodox Serbs have already been converted to Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you know that when an Orthodox Serb converts to Catholicism that automatically everybody in Croatia considers that person to be a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the difference between Serbs and Croats boils down to the question of religion; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Pavelic's Croatia, the Ustasha state, did it wage a policy, the aim of which was to kill a third of the Serbs, to expel another third to Serbia, and to convert the last third to Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Ante Pavelic's policy and the politics he pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. VS-004. Now, The Hague Prosecutors showed you some documents during the proofing sessions, and you stated your views on these documents. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They showed you the declaration on the situation in Yugoslavia of the 28th of October, 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear me? Anyway, they showed you a declaration on the situation in Yugoslavia dated the 28th of October, 1991, and you said that you had never seen that document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is to be found on page 8 of the attachment to your statement of 2006, and then on the basis of that, on the basis of you saying that you had never seen the document, they introduce it along with your testimony as evidence that you had never seen it before and they have it tendered.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the statement that I'd never seen the document until it was placed before me, and we saw here that it was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And for the Brioni joint declaration of the 7th of July, 1991, you also said that you had never seen that document either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't seen that document ever. I wasn't in a position to see it until I came here to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they introduced it as an exhibit as if you had seen it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did see that it was on the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They showed you another list, Epoha, and on the title page there was a picture of Dobrica Cosic, the renowned Serb writer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they misled you to the effect that the text that appeared in the Epoha and that was presented here was written by Dobrica Cosic himself, that he was the author of the text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what -- that's the conclusion I made, that it was a text written by Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Prosecution said that that was the case, and here it says that Dobrica Cosic wrote that article for the third way. Now, was Dobrica Cosic at that convention for a third Yugoslavia at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that. It was a large meeting, and I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But if he was, you would have remembered, because he's such a renowned writer that all us other mere mortals, at that time, barely reached his knees we were so small.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had that kind of authority, so I do believe that I would have noticed if he had been there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They showed you a translation of my interview given to Der Spiegel, the German journal; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that was published in August 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So for it to be published on the 8th of August, the interview would have had to have been given during the month of July; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could conclude that. You can't give an interview after the article's been published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And since I'm talking about my command position there, that must have been before the 1st of August, 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what one could conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever give interviews to foreign correspondents ever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you ever authorise the interview or did you just talk to the journalist and let him leave with your interview and publish what he liked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never gave my authorisation. It was up to the journalist's free will whether they would publish the interview or how they would publish the interview. I didn't authorise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that in the interview they would publish something that you never said or that they mistakenly interpreted your words or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cases like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you say you never saw those interviews published later on because they appeared in the foreign press?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they appeared once and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But when they were published, you didn't really know that they were published and what it said because the newspapers never reached you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on very rare occasions did the newspapers actually reach me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Renate Flottau who was the correspondent of Der Spiegel from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1999, the Serbian Radical Party was in a coalition with Milosevic's party and that we had 15 ministers in the government of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that it was during that period but I can't say whether it was in 1999, but I do remember that you had entered a coalition with Milosevic's party and that you had a significant presence in power and authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that Renate Flottau was officially expelled by our government from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was this case of a journalist being officially asked to leave, but I don't know whether it was Renate Flottau, who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The reason for her expulsion was her subversive activity with regard to the war for Kosovo and Metohija, the NATO aggression, the Albanian terrorists and their rebellions and so on and so forth. You didn't hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now they also showed you some footage here, a fragment from the BBC broadcast "The Death of Yugoslavia", and on that video you can see part of my statement where I say that Milosevic asked us radicals to send volunteers to the front. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember that it was my first meeting with Milosevic in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I say in that interview and it was broadcast on one occasion here. However that's not important if you don't remember that detail. But do you know that Yugoslavia was given ultimatum by the western powers and the Security Council, as far as I remember, that by the 19th of May, 1992, all JNA units should be withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, is it obvious that Milosevic and I were discussing the fate of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time after the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could conclude that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I, during those days, persistently advocated in public that the JNA should not withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we should reject the ultimatum of the Western powers come what may?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Quite obviously Mr. Milosevic and I are discussing the fate of the Serb people after the withdrawal of the JNA. That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could make that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So when I ask him what's going to be -- what's going to happen with the Serbs over there, he says, "Well, send us some volunteers."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail. It was a long time ago after all, and I didn't follow all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm sure you know that the JNA did in fact withdraw on the 19th of May and that in Bosnia-Herzegovina all that was left were the Serbs that were born there and that they formed an army of Republika Srpska. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Therefore, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who after that period of time went could no longer go under JNA organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what one could conclude. I don't know what happened before that. That would be a logical conclusion. If there was no JNA, then it couldn't have organised it over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And if we sent volunteers after that time then they had to go in civilian clothes. They couldn't have worn uniforms. They couldn't have gone bearing arms but they would be transported in civilian clothing as ordinary civilians and then would report to the various commands and be deployed and sent where they were sent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility but I'm not well-versed in affairs of that kind so I can't confirm or refute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You remember that in 1991, I myself wore a camouflage uniform from time to time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I had a pistol on me when I toured the front lines. Sometimes I would have a Kalashnikov, an automatic rifle on me. Sometimes it would be the M-56 automatic rifle depending on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could see you in the media with different weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, the microphone seems to be working again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, after the 19th of May, 1992, and the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you ever see me in uniform after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't claim that I saw you in uniform after that. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you see television footage of me touring Republika Srpska or Republika Srpska Krajina? And I went there several times and held rallies in Serbian Krajina in 1995 for the last time, I was in Okucani too, and I always went wearing civilian clothes. Were you able to see that on television? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that in Okucani when you were there, that you were wearing civilian clothes and when you went to some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I as a citizen of Serbia and a military conscript of the JNA never left Serbia wearing a uniform. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember seeing you later on in uniform, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, we dealt with that set of questions. I'd like to move on to another area and deal with some general circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question which could summarise everything that's been said here, the questions and the answers. Mr. Seselj seems to be asking you to confirm the following: The JNA withdrew in 1992 at a date which we can confirm without any problem. When the JNA withdraws, it seems that Milosevic then asked for volunteers to be sent in. The volunteers would then have arrived on the spot, and these volunteers would then have been integrated by local units called TO units that would have incorporated them in their units. Is that how you perceived things? Is this the way things happened when the JNA withdrew and the volunteers arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one might conclude that. I did not have any insight into the manner of arrival, the methods of recruitment, the issuing of uniforms and weapons. I know that the JNA was leaving at the time and that -- Herzegovina, and that officers went over to the army of Republika Srpska, and one can only conclude that now the volunteers who arrived would belong to the Republika Srpska army because the JNA was no longer there. But I didn't live there, and as a civilian I did not have any insight into the inner workings of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to raise a point. I'm afraid you did not properly understand one segment of my cross-examination. I said in that statement Milosevic asked, but you have to see the context. He didn't ask me officially to send volunteers on behalf of Serbia. When I expressed my fears and my opposition to the withdrawal of the JNA and how the Serbs down there would be able to resist the Croats and the Muslims who had joined forces with the support of the West, he responded, "Well, send us -- you should send more volunteers." Official Serbia had nothing to do with the sending of volunteers, and there's not a shred of evidence that official Serbia participated in that. The OTP has no document and no evidence to show that. It was finished as far as official Serbia was concerned. It was now up to the Serb Radical Party and our people who were desirous of coming to their aid of their brothers across the River Drina. I think this has to be clarified so that this testimony can be reduced to the framework it belongs in because the OTP has been too ambitious presenting evidence through this witness that the witness knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard what has just been clarified. What do you have to say about this? Is this a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- I don't know what else I could say, Your Honour. I didn't have any insight into that. All I can say is that the JNA left. The army that remained reorganised itself as the army of Republika Srpska, and anyone arriving in the area would have to be organised by the army of Republika Srpska, but how this operated I don't know. I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to remark that the witness gave us a fairly clear testimony, and it is for the Trial Chamber to draw its conclusions thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
