utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, we have seven minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll make use of that to deal with another important point concerning the general circumstances. I finished with the crime base now, although the OTP did not have the right to introduce a witness testifying to the crime base in Western Slavonia, but as they did, I had to clarify the issues concerning Vocin, crimes against civilians and everything else, but let me point out that the OTP had no right to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-004, are you aware that Franjo Tudjman was one of the first people in the former Yugoslavia who started publicly challenging the official data on the war crimes committed in World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the present-day regime in Croatia is still doing this and that Stipe Mesic, Ivo Sanader and all the other high-ranking officials are participating in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they're endeavouring for the data that was the official data in the former Yugoslavia to be challenged and to have data that is reduced in numbers accepted as the official data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that when it comes to the number of victims in Jasenovac at the trial in Nuremberg the figure of 700.000 was officially used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the official information up until the war in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that most European states have laws proclaiming it a criminal offence to attempt to reduce the number of victims in World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that this is a highly sensitive issue and that it's banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Usually it is the pro-Nazi forces that want to reduce those numbers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would rather say that it is those whose compatriots who committed those crimes who want to reduce the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Franjo Tudjman, referring to the total number of victims in Jasenovac wanted to reduce that number to 40.000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his aim and his intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Stipe Mesic and the present-day officials in Croatia are trying to reduce the number of victims in Jasenovac to -- between 80 and 100.000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some research in Croatia has come up with those figures, and that's what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Yad Vashem, the big Holocaust museum in Israel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard that according to the official information of Yad Vashem in Jasenovac, 600.000 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Miroslav Krleza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that Miroslav Krleza is one of the greatest Croatian men of letters of all time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that for several decades Miroslav Krleza was the director of the Yugoslav Lexicographic Institute with its headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that the encyclopedia of Yugoslavia which was compiled under his leadership published the information that 500 to 600.000 Serbs, Croats, and Jews were killed in Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of an authors called Jakov Gelo, a demographer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're not aware that he published in 1987, in Zagreb, a book published by Globus entitled "Demographic Changes in Croatia from 1978 to 1981" where he stated that in Jasenovac over 700.000 camp inmates were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this information. I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1961 and 1962 a group of five professors, university professors, including Dr. Ante Pogacnik from the Institute of Forensic Medicine in Ljubljana; Dr. Vida Brodar, professor from Ljubljana; Dr. Ante Predl, a professor of forensic medicine at Zagreb university; Dr. Srboljub Zivanovic, an anthropologist, a professor Emeritus in London and Professor Maric --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is to fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- and they concluded that in the graves that have been investigated alone over 700.000 corpses were found?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go more slowly because the interpreters have difficulty keeping up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My question is: Are you aware that this commission which had a majority of Croats and Slovenes in it concluded based on information from the ground that in those graves that have been investigated over 700.000 corpses were buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were unable to investigate all the graveyards because it's an area that's frequently flooded by the River Sava and many corpses are floated down the Sava. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now 10.00, and we shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've resumed the hearing. It's 20 past 10.00. You have the floor, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-004, have you heard had of Simon Wiesenthal's centre for the investigation and prosecution of war criminals with it's headquarters in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear Mr. Seselj's question, but the interpretation I'm receiving is in English -- or, rather, I'm hearing English in my headset and it's very confusing. Yes, I have heard of Simon Wiesenthal's centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Wiesenthal's centre has an official figure of 600.000 victims of the Jasenovac camp in World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's evident that the precise number will never be known because entire villages were killed, but certainly there were not less than 600.000 victims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's correct that the real number will never be known, and we Serbs who feel victimised believe in that figure of 600.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned that a large number of your close family members were killed in Jasenovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in Gradiska, the camp of Stara Gradiska which belonged to the Jasenovac camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Seventeen members of your close family were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventeen only on my father's side, on my father's side alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This will not reveal the witness's identity. You don't have to intervene. I am taking that into account. I will have a few questions towards the end of my cross-examination, and I will tell you then when it refers to personal information, but this information will not identify the witness in public. Do you agree, Witness 004? This is information that cannot reveal your identity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So both your father and your mother suffered a similar fate. They were small children at the time of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Pavelic's Ustasha state, as part of its official policy, took away small children from Serbs who had been liquidated and gave them to Croatian families for adoption, education, care, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were several tens of thousands of such children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Most of these children were so small that they had no idea who their father was, who their mother was, and it would be very hard for them to discover this after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This did -- this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course there are many honourable and honest Croats, and your parents were lucky to be cared for by such people. However, there were others who immediately had those children convert to Catholicism, gave them other names and so on. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Another detail concerning your statement given to the OTP. You mentioned here allegedly that on the 19th of December, volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party got drunk in Masicka Sagovina and were killed by Croats. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about this, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did you hear from that they were drunk and that's why they were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that because that's a date connected with Saint Nicolas, who is an important Serbian saint, and they were celebrating. That was the version of the story I heard, that they were celebrating this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to what I learned, in the village of Masicka Sagovina it's Djurdjevdan which is usually celebrated. St. George is celebrated as the patron saint of most of the inhabitants of the village. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that might be true, but the patron saint of those people might have been Saint Nicolas. Maybe they were celebrating with a friend whose patron saint it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And can you recall who told you they were drunk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that on that day Croatian paramilitary formations attacked Masicka Sagovina with a large force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that date there was a widespread offensive on the territory of Western Slavonia from Pakrac onward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we move into private session for a few seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm taking the floor because earlier on Mr. Seselj put questions to the witness about orphans, Serb orphans, that were allegedly adopted and given to Croatian families during the Second World War. It's something I was not aware of, and it may be true or not. But I'm putting myself in the shoes -- or in the place of Croats who would listen to this and who would then start wondering about their own relationship with their own parents, about their own family connections. Therefore, I would like to consult my colleagues to see whether we should not redact this part of the proceedings because we still have time to issue an order for a redaction. Such adoption issues are always very sensitive, and some people listening to this might find this extremely traumatic. People might start asking questions to their parents. So I'd like to consult my fellow Judges to see what we'll do about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a well-known fact described in a large number of books, newspaper serials. It's no secret. Almost all these children, except for those who were small babies, did try to find out about their origins after the war and with great difficulty they would learn about their background. Unless you tell the public -- no one will be upset by this in the public because it is a well-known fact, and I think the witness is aware that it's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After considering the matter we only have one question to put to the witness. Witness, you've heard the questions put to you by Mr. Seselj about this matter. Do you believe that -- or personally does this have an impact on your own situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Those children, if they are still alive, are now aged about 70. There are many people, most notably the children of Mount Kozara, who ended up that way. Many were raised by other families. Some learned about their real parents, others didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Trial Chamber decides to keep all that part of the transcript public. We're now going to go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I demand that this part of the secret session, while you were still deliberating, be made public. The public needs to know the dilemmas faced by the Trial Chamber. It's very important, and it doesn't identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will respond to this application of yours later. Please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard that in the Jasenovac camp more than 20.000 small Serbian children were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That information circulated in the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Ustasha government of Ante Pavelic took a number of children of Serbian parents who were killed and gave them to be raised by Croatian families to become Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was their objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us go back to Masicka Sagovina. You heard from someone - you don't know who - that the volunteers had got drunk. Do you know that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in Masicka Sagovina were engaged in a blocking defence until all the population had managed to pull out and the Territorial Defence, too, that they sacrificed themselves to save others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the fighting. I didn't know about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that on that day 11 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were killed while a number were wounded and captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of those who were killed and I know that some were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that among the captured there was one girl, Dusica Nikolic who, after a while, served as an MP from the Serbian Radical Party in the Assembly of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In a Croatian prison she was subjected to the most cruel torture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there was not a single captured volunteer who was actually prosecuted, volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party? They were all released after a while without any charges.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you mentioned Dusica Nikolic who was an MP, and you stated that she was imprisoned in a Croatian prison, that she was brutally tortured, and so on and so forth. I do not know whether this is an established fact or not, but what I'm wondering is whether Ms. Dusica Nikolic would agree for us to be discussing her situation openly. That's my problem. Can you confirm me that this is an established fact? Has this been investigated? Has there been a judgement about this? Because I can imagine that Ms. Nikolic would not want this to be discussed in public.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Dusica Nikolic lives in Belgrade. About the torture in the Croatian prison she spoke a lot, even in the National Assembly of Serbia and gave several interviews to newspapers. Dusica Nikolic will be my defence witness, and here in the courtroom she will testify in public because I won't have a single secret witness, and she will testify publicly about everything she went through in the Croatian prison. You see, the witness had heard about this case too. If he -- if he hadn't heard -- if it hadn't been discussed publicly, he wouldn't have heard about it. And there was not a single prosecution. They never prosecute criminals unless they are pressured into it by someone from the outside. All their criminals go scot-free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to move back into open session and all this part of the transcript can be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We are now going back to a number of details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait a moment. The registrar needs to announce that we're in public session, in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We are in open session. Let me say that we were in private session and we mentioned the situation of Ms. Dusica Nikolic. Mr. Seselj announced that she would be testifying as a Defence witness. As a result, the portion of the transcript that was recorded in private session is now going to become public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991, the Vance Plan was accepted, the plan to deploy UN troops in the territory of the Serbian Krajina, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and the JNA was to pull out from these areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Serbs anywhere, any time after the deployment of the UNPROFOR, restart on their own initiative armed actions against Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no armed actions. All I know is that in some areas of Western Slavonia some groups made deep incursions across the separation lines, and there were several ambushes killing policemen, and there were some civilian victims too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you talking about Croatian groups making incursions into Serbian territory or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I just said was Serbian groups making incursions across the separation lines. They went to visit their villages, ran into a police patrol which they liquidated, and sometimes they seized vehicles and kidnapped civilians, Croats in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it was individual incidents, individuals doing something of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While the weaponry of the army of the Serbian Krajina was under lock and key.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One key was in the hands of the UNPROFOR, and the other key was in the hands of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That applied to heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the staffs of Territorial Defence still functioned, although the employees came to work in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1992 and early 1993. Later on, the staffs got uniformed again, and until 1995 they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they took up arms again only when Croats started attacking certain UN safe areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the case of Maslenica, which happened in January 1993. Later on our leadership in Western Slavonia changed. The attitude changed, and that's when the staffs took up their role again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that in September 1993 there was an attack by Croat forces on the Medak pocket in Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that attack were all civilians who were found there killed, and all the villages and UN safe areas were burned, Citluk, Divoselo and Pocitelj. They were completely destroyed these three villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that the UNPROFOR general Jean Cot stated on that occasion that he had been to the area and found no signs of life, human or animal, that the destruction by Croatian forces was systematic, deliberate and complete?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You spoke about Western Slavonia and the destruction of Serbian villages. What is the total number of Serbian villages burned, devastated, destroyed by Croats after December 1991 when they captured the greatest part of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 165 villages were completely devastated and destroyed in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Plus another 20 or so that were partially destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1995, on the 1st of May, the Croats mounted an operation known publicly as Operation Flash; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The purpose of the operation was to take hold of all Western Slavonia and to expel the Serbian population from there; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those areas of Western Slavonia were officially under the protection of the UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On two occasions Mr. Seselj asked you to confirm that these territories were under the protection of UNPROFOR. What does it mean, in your opinion, what does this protection mean? What was it all about? What did it entail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that area, Your Honours, the forces of the UN, both military and police, were deployed. They supervised and controlled those areas in order to prevent the kind of war between Serbs and Croats that occurred in 1991. In the meantime, a UN Security Council Resolution changed their mandate, so in end 1995 it was called UNCRO a protection belt in Croatia which encouraged the Croatian forces to believe they could attack it whereas in fact they shouldn't have. It was under UN protection. The UN forces were supposed to protect it, to prevent conflict. And they should have warned the population at the time that Croatian forces are preparing an attack so that the population could prepare themselves and move rather than suffer the destruction and killing that they did in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you, did UNPROFOR have a mandate to oppose militarily any type of attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a delicate issue. I'll try to shed some light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely because it's delicate that I'm putting that question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Right. When I was negotiating with the UNPROFOR in 1992, and when we in Western Slavonia demilitarised, handing over our heavy weaponry to be under double key, the only armed force was the police carrying short barrels, that is, pistols in Western Slavonia, we got guarantees from Commander Zabala, commander of Sector West, who said that in case of attack by the Croatian army, they would respond and protect that area from the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was the commander who gave you that guarantee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander was General Zabala from the Argentinian battalion. In 1992, we got a written guarantee from him, and sometime on the 2nd September, 1992, Marrack Goulding, the under-secretary of the United Nations, came to the area to congratulate us on the implementation of the Vance Plan and supported our activities and actions and encouraged us to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that you received a written document from that Argentinian general and he had stated that he would intervene if your sector was attacked; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how it was, Your Honour, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue my clarification? In 1993, an order was issued by our Serbian commander, a general from Banija, General Novakovic, that we in Western Slavonia, who had a total of five tanks, should attack Novska and Gradiska, that is neighbouring towns under Croatian control because an offensive was to be launched from there. An urgent meeting was then held between the civilian authorities and the UNPROFOR where we civilians imposed a ban on moving those tanks because General Zabala had promised to protect us if a conflict occurs. And then again those weapons placed again under control in those delicate moments. We had those guarantees from him and that's why we acted in the spirit of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And afterwards when the Croats attacked, no one kept their promises, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in 1995 -- in the meantime I had spent time in prison. I was no longer part of the authorities. I was a regular citizen. And in 1995, when another all-out offensive of the Croatian forces occurred, the units of the UNPROFOR simply moved, pulled out from their locations, but one Serbian unit stopped one of their units. And through that unit we established contact with representatives of the United Nations in order to start negotiations on a truce which we managed to establish only after 24 hours, thanks only to that one patrol. Because when the Croatian artillery started firing, they all pulled out, and that was the only one patrol that helped us establish contact with the UNPROFOR that resulted eventually in a truce after 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Croatian army in Operation Flash kill Serb civilians that it came across?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases where the Serb civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were -- did many Serb civilians die going towards Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot was said about this and I heard from people who broke through during that event. They said there were many dead and many wounded and an investigation was launched but the exact figure was never established because the traces were done away with. And there were quite a lot of people who either had someone or didn't have anybody to ask after them. So we don't actually know the exact figure of the number of civilians killed during the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that the column of civilians was attacked severely by the Croatian artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Croatian air force, was it included in the bombing of civilians who were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct that the motorway used by the civilians in their withdrawal was so full of blood that afterwards they used hoses and detergents to wash the blood away from the asphalt surface?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this on the road from Okucani to Stara Gradiska. It's not a motorway, it's a road leading directly to Stara Gradiska or Bosanska Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who lieutenant colonel Harambasic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is lieutenant colonel -- was lieutenant Harambasic commander of the Serb forces in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did lieutenant colonel Harambasic negotiate with the Croats through the mediation of the United Nations to have his unit hand over its weapons to UNPROFOR so that the Serbs without weapons could withdraw from the area and that 1.500 soldiers should withdraw and 4.000 civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were negotiations about that for a surrender, and I took part in those talks and the weapons were indeed handed over, and it was agreed that the soldiers who wished to leave could do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that as soon as the Serbs lay down their arms, surrendered their arms, Croatian artillery opened fire on them and demanded unconditional surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all those negotiations that went on for some time, there was supposed to be a final round of talks which was postponed three times, and near us negotiators there were representatives of the European observers too. They attended the negotiations throughout. And when the final agreement was postponed, what happened was that there was shelling, sudden shelling. And during that shelling the news reached us that unconditional surrender was being called for, unconditional surrender of civilians because there were no more soldiers under arms at the time. They'd all taken off their uniforms and were civilians and waiting for further developments. And then the surrender itself took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What happened to the soldiers when they surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, almost all of them ranging in age between 18 and 60, and there were even people who were 80 years old who were arrested and taken to prisons in Bjelovar, Varazdin, Pozega, Osijek, and so on. There were private prisons at the time, too, or that's what people said and quite large number of them, especially in Varazdin, were physically mistreated and some succumbed to their wounds. Some were beaten up. Many later on took a long time to recover after the mistreatment, and a smaller number were released one day after another, after they had been interrogated I assume. And when they returned to Pakrac in the buses, the police made them slap each other so you would have two brothers slapping each other on orders from the police. And when these people arrived where these soldiers were, many of them left Western Slavonia because they were afraid of what was about to happen, and those who stayed on were abused overnight. There's the village of Brusnik which was an example in point where the policemen stormed their homes at night and made them lick salt, lick salt. They abused them, and then they left the area and went towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that in Operation Flash a total of 20.000 Serbs were expelled from the territory of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a figure that we had at the time. It was 15.000 around Okucani and 5.000, almost 6.000 in the Pakrac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that at that time only 1.000 Serbs stayed on in the territory of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after those events and the exodus or, rather, the departure of the people, we made a list of people that remained and those who were missing, and the figure was that about 1.700 remained, some 1.700 Serbs remained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, it's all right now. I was very careful in handling the microphone so I don't know what went wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But is it true that the Serb houses at the time were looted and set alight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the territory of Okucani and up there around Pakrac where we stayed there was looting but there was no setting fire to houses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that the remaining Serb civilians were mistreated in large numbers and some of them were even killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't mass killing. There was killing. People were killed and nobody was held responsible still, but they were mistreated, and I personally attended one such instance in a village around Pakrac where I happened to be. They asked me to go there and take them out because they had -- were having a lot of problems. They were being mistreated. So when I returned, that very moment I called --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Only one short observation. All these events happened in 1995. That is far behind the time frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj. What is the relevance of what happened in 1995 as against what you wish to prove?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these events depict the relationship of the Croatian authorities towards Serb civilians, and that relationship was a continuous one identical for a five-year period. So that's the relevance of it. That's why this is important. It is important to show that the Serbs over there had no other way out but to resist Croatian attacks by taking up arms. Their ultimate fate is best proof and evidence that that was the only way out. They didn't manage to be victorious and preserve their villages and houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a question to put to you. As in 1995, well, as we've said, this is not part of the indictment, but you were present in the Pakrac area, and you therefore witnessed the Flash offensive that was launched by the Croatian army. It seems according to the questions that were put to you and according to your answers that 20.000 Serbs allegedly left the area and were driven out. This is what I'm interested in. I'm trying to understand why all these people left and why according to the census only 1.700 Serbs were left. Your neighbours or the people in the area, when these people left, they left because they were afraid of what was about to happen or because orders had been given to the effect that they should leave? Or was their departure connected to a feeling of panic which is more than understandable in such situation or was it a concerted action which meant that these people had to leave? What kind of light can you shed on this, because you witnessed all of this, and why didn't you yourself leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Western Slavonia was specific as a region because the way of life there was normal. There were contacts with the other side, with the Croats, that is. There were check-points at a number of places where family and friends could meet. Then there was the motorway and the Serbs left -- or, rather, the Serbs went to the Croatian petrol pumps to get fuel. Then there were intentional situations of incident, and a Serb was killed at one of such petrol pump with a knife. And to quote an example, well, there was this dead man lying by the petrol pump killed by a Croat. Everybody saw that, but everybody went on tanking up. They didn't pay that much attention. They didn't think it would present any great fear. But later on the Serb police closed off the motorway to prevent this point of contact and they said that this was to prevent further killing. Now, when an all-out offensive broke out with strong artillery and tank forces being engaged, then certainly there was panic and fear among the population so that they should not fare the same way as they did in Maslenica [indiscernible] pocket. And they left the area in a panic. Those of us who remained in the Pakrac area we were under siege. We were in an enclave under siege for four days and I said a moment ago that it was thanks to the patrol that was held back and we were able to establish contact with the United Nations and negotiated for four days. And as a group, four and a half to 5.000 there were -- people there until -- we were there until the 4th of May. Now after being beaten up in the prisons and all the mistreatment, many people left. And part of those people, military conscripts left because they thought they might be mobilised and sent to the war against other -- in other areas of Krajina. They didn't feel safe and secure. Now, we tried to prevail upon the people to stay on and to take over the new documents of the Croatian authorities and to continue our struggle for our rights. We didn't come across fruitful ground because there was general chaos. People had been beaten and they didn't believe anyone anymore. And I know that I talked to the European observers, and they said it is your human right to fight for that, to continue living in the area, to -- win your rights. And if you leave, it means you have given up on your rights and what you are owed. So my colleagues and I decided to stay on, but I can tell you that it was very difficult period because all those who had remained to the present day - and that's 12 or 13 years on - cannot find employment in state institutions. They can only find employment privately. We still do not have guaranteed civilians' rights, although we do have religious rights, but there were difficulties after Operation Flash. I know that on Christmas extremists stormed our church and threatened us and so on. So these were very difficult times and, as I say, it's still difficult to live there today. You don't have the right to work, to employment; and if you don't have the right to employment, you don't have the means of a livelihood and existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your rather comprehensive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Having mentioned the right to employment and right to work, is it true that the Croatian authorities took away tenants' rights to all Serbs who were expelled from Croatia or out of fear left of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a well-known fact. It's only the Serbs that lost their tenant's rights in the Republic of Croatia during 1991. If they had not spent six months living in a particular apartment, many left because they were threatened. Many left because of fear. Many were evicted from their flats when they went out to work and when they came back home, they found somebody else living in their flats and they would change the locks and wouldn't allow the tenants to go to their flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since the Trial Chamber does not know what this property right means and tenants' rights, let me explain it. Tenants' rights are a part of property rights which was specifically developed in Communist Yugoslavia; isn't that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Communist Yugoslavia people, for the most part, did not have the possibility of building their own houses or buying their own flats. Those were few and far between; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was no need because you would get a socially owned flat and you would deal with your housing problem that way. You were assigned a socially owned flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To continue along those lines, this happened in the following way: Everybody employed would set aside a part of their salary to what was called the housing fund; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it was from these housing funds that flats were be purchased in socially owned enterprises and so on and then they would be allocated to the employees on the basis of a list of priorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when somebody was once assigned a flat, nobody could take that flat away from him but he did not have the right to sell it, so the flats could be inherited by their immediate family members and descendants. So this was a form of limited tenants' rights. You can't sell the flat but nobody, on the other hand, could take the flat away from you; is that right? Is that how things worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth of.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, the Tudjman authorities took away these rights from Serbs unscrupulously who had left their flats for more than six months and this was contrary to the Constitution and contrary to the law right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they did this only to the Serbs. If Croats were absent from their flat for even a few years, nobody would question their tenants' rights; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have just one more question related to 1995 and then we'll go back to something that is far more relevant in terms of the indictment. In August 1995, a new large-scale Croatian operation against Serbian Krajina took place under the name of Storm, Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in organising this operation an allegedly private but close to the Pentagon organisation was invoked, the IMPR, that they were resorted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact name but I do know that a private organisation was used to help in the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the American air force incapacitated all Serb radar systems before the Croatian operation was launched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Americans thereby incapacitated the command posts of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that then mean that we're not only dealing with Croatia but it was an American aggression against Serbian Krajina which is under the protection of the United Nations in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I heard it was assisted by -- or, rather, Croatia was assisted by NATO Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that during Operation Storm about 200.000 Serbs were expelled from the western part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that on that occasion 22.000 Serb houses were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the figure that was seriously quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of the organisation called Veritas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who heads Veritas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know but I can't remember the name now. I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that that organisation, Veritas, established that at least 1.791 Serbs were killed or went missing in the course of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that of that number 996 Serb civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that number from Veritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that out of that 996 Serb civilians 449 women were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That Veritas information is also well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that 11 Serb children were killed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number also has been published by Veritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the year 1991. Do you recall that the authorities of Western Slavonia, in April 1992, established that in the course of 1991, 4.118 Serb houses were destroyed in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that that same document contains the information that in that period, that is in 1991, 27 Serb Orthodox churches were destroyed on the territory of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware of Boutros-Ghali's report from May 1993 according to which from Croatia beyond the -- that is, not in the Republic of Serb Krajina, 251.000 Serbs were expelled from the towns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that but if that's in Boutros-Ghali's report it can easily be established. I don't recall the precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dr. Svetozar Livade, a professor of Zagreb university, who has patiently dealt with many years with the persecution of Serbs under Tudjman's regime, are you aware of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that in some publications and books he published specific information as to the different ways in which the Croatian authorities under Tudjman and later on persecuted Serbs and what kind of discriminatory measures are still being applied against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of those books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, as in the course of the examination-in-chief the Vance Plan was admitted into evidence, that the Vance Plan envisaged exclusively negotiations as a means of solving the problems between the Serb Krajina and the Republic of Croatia without pre-judging the outcome of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it not obvious that the Vance Plan was in fact a trick played on you Serbs? We all accepted that plan trusting in the United Nations, and it turned out later on that we were tricked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result turned out to be bad. Let me mention that the leadership in Knin did not make use of all their opportunities to negotiate. They may have missed their chance. I'm not saying things wouldn't have turned out the same in the end but they did not seize the opportunity of having good quality negotiations to search for a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. You mentioned Boutros-Ghali's report dated May 1993, and Dr. Svetozar Livada's publication, who was a professor in Zagreb. These two documents seem to indicate that 251.000 people were expelled. Why do you not present these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the OTP has those documents at their disposal. As early as 2006 under Rule 68(i), the OTP disclosed to me a huge pile of texts by Professor Svetozar Livada. They have those documents. I am cross-examining the witness here. It's not for me to prove that I'm innocent. I'm proving that the indictment is false and that there is no evidence against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the problem is that you submit your theory, but if the Judges do not have the documents in support of your case we will not be satisfied with the mere question and answer. In that case, your case will not be corroborated by any documentary evidence. You say yes, but these documents are in the hands of the Prosecution, but if the Prosecution does not tender them into evidence, we have a problem. I have told you already. I have told you this a few days ago, and I am telling you again. It may be important for us to know that after this Flash operation, tempest operation, there were large movements of population from Western Slavonia and Serb Krajina, but if this is not supported by any documents, this will just remain on the transcript. Technically speaking, it is very easy for you to do. You could have said, "Witness, let me present you with Boutros-Ghali's report in which it says so-and-so," and the witness then says,"yes, it's written in the document," and it is then tendered into evidence. "Let me present Dr. Livade's book." The witness will say, "Yes, and the book says such-and-such," and then you ask for this to be tendered into evidence. This is what I wanted to tell you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I had an assistant here I could present all this to you. As I'm working on my own, I am preparing for my defence in the way I consider is best for my interests. If I had my legal advisors and my case managers here, it would all look different probably. They would immediately be handing these documents to me. I cannot carry full boxes with me every day. My briefcase is quite heavy, and in the course of the examination-in-chief of this witness not a single charge against me was put forward. This witness is not alleging anything against me. That's why I'm discussing general circumstances with him. If I had had any reason to vehemently oppose his allegations that it would all look different, but you can see that he's not alleging anything against me and we have been public enemies for 15 or 16 years. We lashed out at each other in public, and we couldn't bear to look at one another. I am bringing only the most important documents here. The witness confirmed that those documents are in existence and that's sufficient for me. Allow me to be in charge of my own defence. I don't need Boutros-Ghali's plan to prove false allegations against me in the indictment. When we come to specifics, to concrete matters, then I'll bring documents. I can't deal so intensely with these peripheral matters but I want to make use of my time in the best possible way, so please allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. VS-004, that Franjo Tudjman, in 1992, on the occasion of the anniversary of the declaration of independence, the first anniversary, declared on Jelacic square in Zagreb that there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it? Do you remember that statement he made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that statement of his. I don't know whether he stated that in the place you mentioned, but I know he did say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the statement itself is more important than the place it was uttered, but according to my information it was on the square the Croats called Jelacic place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tudjman then say that they, the Croatian leaders, could only gain independence through war? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Tomislav Mercep killed Serb civilians and tortured and mistreated them in Vukovar before the JNA entered into a conflict with Croatian paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that these crimes have been alleged against him and his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These crimes of his, did they escalate to such an extent that the Croatian authorities finally had to remove him from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tomislav Mercep then arrive in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tomislav Mercep, with his group of armed para-soldiers commit heinous crimes in Pakracka Poljana?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those crimes in Pakracka Poljana have been alleged against him and his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Has there been an investigation of Tomislav Mercep after many years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the chief witness, an insider witness who described all the ways in which they killed Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard and read about it, but I can't recall his name at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was his last name Bajramovic or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that witness against Mercep, was he killed later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a witness was killed and another witness died. I can't remember whether Bajramovic is the one who was killed or the one died, but I do know that one was killed and that one died, of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that throughout the war and throughout the existence of the Republika Srpska Krajina, the Croats in many places in that area lived quite peacefully without any harassment? For example, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about Knin, that they lived there normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were incidents, I don't deny that. Sometimes there were problems, but those who wanted to live in Republika Srpska Krajina were not prevented from doing so by the authorities and there was no policy of expelling Croats from the area. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later on when the Republika Srpska Krajina was established and the civilian authorities began operating, I think they could live in peace without persecution, but there was persecution and killing and burning in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this persecution was not organised by the authorities. There were incidents among the people. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did happen. If more than one person is killed it's more than just an incident. It's more like an operation. I don't know that there were orders that this should be done. There were moments when extremists wanted to take revenge for reasons only they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We've already established that on the 19th and 20 of November, 1991, I visited Western Slavonia. Do you know that on the 20th I returned to Banja Luka in the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the second day you went back, so you probably did go to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was supposed to be met by a helicopter in Banja Luka on the 21st. Are you aware that that night officials of the Banja Luka Serbian Democratic Party took me to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know why I went to Knin so urgently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there I had a conflict with Captain Dragan, Dragan Vasiljkovic who called himself Captain Dragan in public?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that conflict between you and Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that a personal conflict or did we have differences concerning the Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge which came through the media, I think you had a conflict because of his manner of operating in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that earlier on he had been expelled from the territory of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something about that, but I didn't know precisely what happened because it was far away from where I was and I didn't have any possibility of establishing the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not aware that in November he returned and started agitating among the soldiers to topple the government of Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that from the media but nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The OTP here showed footage of my conflict with Captain Dragan in Benkovac, and you were shown footage of a conversation I had later, after that, with soldiers on different issues and only a short clip was played. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember when I tried to convince them that they should respect the officers and some of them interrupted me saying they were Communists, that I had -- well, I had to convince them to wear a helmet because it's much more dangerous to wage war without a helmet. There were more woundings, especially in the Kas [phoen] terrain. It would be enough for a shell to land on the stone, for a piece of stone to hit a soldier in the head and kill him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw you, yes, trying to convince them about the officers and of course I didn't see the entire footage so I can't interpret your words, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude something else that I insisted on discipline by insisting on their obeying their officers because it was primarily a matter of discipline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude from my manner of speaking and from their behaviour that these were not volunteers of the SRS, because volunteers of the SRS would have kept silent while I was speaking? They would have shown me more respect. I had to tell them to be quiet while I was speaking. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I recognised the man sitting next to you, and judging by their voices and their accents these were local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So these were people from the Knin Krajina, from Benkovac and the surrounding area. You were able to see that. So if I were talking to soldiers who were not volunteers of the SRS but it's evident that I was advocating discipline, could you draw that conclusion from the footage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I concluded that you asked them to trust the JNA officers and have confidence in them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Seselj, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To have confidence in the JNA as the only regular army which had freed itself from its Communist ideological shackles. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the territory of Croatia there was a large number of camps and prisons in which Serb civilians were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard mostly about Western Slavonia, but there were also such camps in other places and in towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What Croatian camps do you know of in Western Slavonia where the Croats kept imprisoned Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about Pakrac, Daruvar, Pozega, Slatina, Gradiska, Novska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, kindly pause before answering questions put to you by Mr. Seselj, because otherwise the interpreters find it difficult to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in a very small area of Western Slavonia there was an enormous, I would say, number of camps where Croatian authorities kept Serbian civilians imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost in every larger settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear about the methods of torture they used against those imprisoned Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard they were mistreated, beaten, that they were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that electrical cables were used most often to beat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you -- did you hear about torture with the low voltage electrical shocks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear there were quite a few cases when imprisoned Serb civilians were ordered to cut each other's ears and then eat them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read about that in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those were statements of survivors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of the survivors from Kipa village, I believe, in the Pakrac fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree when we look at the map of Croatia and bear in mind the ethnic composition in towns and villages that it was much harder for Serbs where there was the smallest number of them than in places where there were lots of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where Serbs were the fewest, they were -- they had the hardest time with the discriminatory measures of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said already that the area of the entire Western Slavonia was severely victimised in the World War II. Did other areas suffer as well in Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banija and Kordun were the hardest hit of all areas, followed by Western Slavonia, followed by Lika and that part of Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I suppose you know that both Banija and Kordun were strongholds of partisans in World War II. There were very few Chetniks there, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Banija and Kordun were known partisan areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were Chetniks in Lika and Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in parts thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that villages in Eastern Slavonia, around Vukovar and Osijek, were also severely victimised in World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in World War II the operation forced conversion to Catholicism of Serbs was implemented to the greatest degree in Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that entire Serb villages such as Okutaj [phoen] in Eastern Slavonia were forced to accept Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that it happened in the largest measure in the Djakovica bishopry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that the new Tudjman authorities with amendment 68 to the constitution of Croatia completely abolished the Cyrillic as one of the official scripts in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which amendment exactly it was, but I know that the Cyrillic was abolished as a script when Tudjman came into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The resistance of Serbs in Western Slavonia to Tudjman's regime, was it spontaneous or was it organised, encouraged, instigated from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a complex issue. I'll try to answer truthfully. The Serbs in Western Slavonia had misgivings about Tudjman's authority, his behaviour, his rhetorics, the provocations that ensued. There followed mistrust and fear. And I remember at all meetings we had about constitutional amendments and at the meeting in Okucani we had a professor of constitutional law present because we wanted to speak technically and professionally about constitutional amendments, people only shouted, "Give us arms, give us arms," because they were so frightened seeing the new Croatian army on television. You couldn't talk to them. They were just demanding weapons. It was already a psychosis. They believed that only weapons will save them because nothing else is left. As such, they did eventually organise themselves and organised their staffs but whether in doing so they had somebody's assistance and help in organising, I don't know. I know that it was not my role, and I had no influence from outside. It was not my role to organise anything -- to organise anything militarily, but I also know that I suffered problems because I tried to negotiate with Tudjman from other people who were more extreme, who considered me as a traitor. I know that many people believed that there was no point in negotiating. It was a battle lost in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1995, when Western Slavonia was captured, part of Serbian Krajina was occupied and Eastern Slavonia was involved in negotiations about peaceful, allegedly peaceful integration into Croatia, the Croatians falsely accused many Serbs of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were indictments mainly raised in 1992 and 1993, issued mainly in the absence of the people concerned, and I know that many of us were called in by the police for interviews and some were prosecuted. Those were collective indictments without much supporting material or evidence, so that people who later tried to come back to Croatia to continue living there, they would be arrested, investigated, and later released, which indicates there was no evidence of their responsibility. This is still going on in Croatia. Nothing is known exactly. And I must say for the sake of people who are still in prison serving sentences of many years are innocent, although they were convicted to 20 years imprisonment because there was no fair trial. There was no proper defence. The witnesses who testified against them were political. And these convictions were made based on indictments from 1992 and 1993 without supporting evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that Croatian authorities indicted Serbs on purpose, falsely, investigated and imprisoned some of them to discourage Serbs from coming back to their property in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We who dealt with the problem came to that conclusion, and through the international community we tried to put pressure on Croatia to stop with those mass indictments, to stop intimidating people, and to bring to justice instead those people who are really responsible so that people who had nothing to do with the crimes could feel free and could continue to live there. But this is still a problem, and it's still being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, tell me about the rest of the Serbs who live in Croatia. There are very few of them. How do they feel in their hearts when it happens, for instance, that Miro Bajramovic, who is one of Mercep's men, admits publicly that he had slit the throats of 72 Serbs, including 9 women, and the Croatian court then acquits him for lack of evidence? How does a Serb react to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter of indifference to them. They know many things that happened, and they feel bitter that the Croatian authorities are so ineffectual and do not treat perpetrators fairly or equally. When the crimes were against Croatians, the trials are quick; and when the crimes were against Serbs, they always don't have enough evidence, things don't move very far or very fast. But they feel helpless they can't change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You probably remember the large rally of Serbian people in a place called Srb on the 25th July 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember I was there too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember you came to the rally. And some people addressed me, too, thinking that I am the same thing that you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean that somebody mistook you for me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people -- some people found a resemblance, although you were not so politically active by that time in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the only resemblance is glasses, because I'm much fatter and much taller.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these people probably are the only ones who know why they made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I hope you don't mind my joke. You don't -- do you remember, did I speak about that meeting -- at that meeting, at that rally? I was just an observer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember you didn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that that rally adopted the declaration of the Serbian people in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That declaration was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I will interpret now briefly the gist of that declaration, and you will confirm whether I did it well or not. Is it the case that Serb political leaders offered to the gathered Serbian people for acclamation three basic positions. One, if Croatia remains within Federal Yugoslavia, Serbs require only cultural autonomy. Two, if Yugoslavia is to turn into a confederation, Serbs then insist on territorial autonomy. Three, if Croatia is seceding from Yugoslavia, Serbs are seceding from Croatia and remain with Yugoslavia. Is this a good interpretation of that declaration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was that general demand of the rally and the then political representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that the basic policy that was later the guiding policy of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please. With respect to the second point, are you talking about a federation or a confederation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second point was a federation -- no, no. That was the first point. If Yugoslavia remains a federation, Serbs want only cultural autonomy, protection for their script, language, cultural heritage.
